title: Invertible Logits Transformation for Accuracy-Preserving Post-Hoc Uncertainty Calibration
claim: The learned scalar transformation departs systematically from identity in dataset-specific ways, and it stays stable regardless of calibration set size.
layout: 3 panels in a row, shared legend on top, shaded deviation from identity
description: Three line plots sit side by side, one each for (a) CIFAR-10, (b) CIFAR-100 and (c) ImageNet. A shared legend above them lists a gray dashed identity line y=x, an orange dashed curve for val=1000 and a thick red solid curve for val=5000. In every panel the x-axis is the input logit and the y-axis is the calibrated logit. The two learned curves nearly overlap, apart from small deviations in the tails. The area between each curve and the identity line is shaded: red where the curve falls below identity on CIFAR-10, and a mix of blue and red on CIFAR-100 and ImageNet. CIFAR-10 compresses large logits, a pattern that suggests it corrects overconfidence. CIFAR-100 and ImageNet expand the logits. The eye goes first to the thick red S-shaped curves and the shaded regions.
caption: Learned scalar transformation fθ on (a) CIFAR-10, (b) CIFAR-100, and (c) ImageNet (ResNet-50). Orange dashed: fθ fitted on val 1 000; red solid: fθ fitted on val 5 000. The nearperfect overlap confirms that InvLT is robust to calibration set size. Gray dashed: identity y = x; shaded regions: deviation from identity.
abstract: Post-hoc calibration aligns a classifier's predicted confidences with its empirical accuracy without retraining. An ideal calibrator should correct nonlinear miscalibration, scale gracefully to large label spaces, and preserve the original predictions; existing methods typically violate at least one of these properties---temperature scaling lacks expressivity, more flexible parametric alternatives introduce parameters that grow with the number of classes $C$, and other expressive methods do not preserve the rank ordering of class scores and may alter the predicted class. We propose \textbf{Invertible Logits Transformation (InvLT)}, which applies a learned scalar MLP $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ element-wise to the pre-softmax logits. Sharing $f$ across all logit dimensions makes the parameter count independent of $C$. Monotonicity of $f$---and hence preservation of the argmax prediction---is softly encouraged via a paired inverse network rather than enforced through the numerical integration required by prior monotone calibrators; this avoids their computational overhead while empirically preserving the original classification accuracy in every setting we evaluate. Across standard image classification benchmarks and a range of architectures, InvLT consistently outperforms a broad set of post-hoc baselines on standard calibration metrics.
